periods.activity_title: Entering the Space Station: Pre-Reading and First Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.205): paired discussion on feathered friends and pets in space.
Let us read (p.206): complete consonant-only words by inserting missing vowels.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading pair discussion from “Let us read” (p.205): who is a feathered friend, and could one go to space? Take brief whole-class share-outs to activate curiosity about the story's setting.

Teacher reads the story aloud, pages 205–210, with students following in their textbooks; pause at key moments — Claribel's first appearance, her zero-gravity loops — to let the scene register before moving on.

Work through the vowel-insertion vocabulary activity from “Let us read” (p.206) as a quick paired exchange: students fill in REGULATION, FORBID, FUSE, ABRUPTLY, CONFESS, DIETITIAN, then verify aloud with the class.
Teacher-led discussion: what do students now know about Sven, Claribel, and the space station? Elicit two or three observations and post key words on the board to consolidate the shared read.

periods.teacher_notes: The story opens by noting that no regulation forbade pets, a detail that sets up the ethical and practical tension students will trace through the narrative. A common difficulty at this stage is confusing Sven's personal curiosity with an official experiment — make the distinction explicit during the shared read. Students who have not yet encountered science fiction may need a brief orienting remark about the space-station setting before reading begins.

periods.activity_title: Claribel in Crisis: Comprehension and Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.209): four brief-answer questions on Sven's motive and Claribel's adaptation.
Let us discuss (p.211): true/false statements about the alarm failure and Claribel's role.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.212): read Extract 1 on Sven's construction work and attempt the four questions independently.

time_bands.activity: Brief teacher recap of the story events read aloud previously — Claribel's smuggling aboard, her zero-gravity adaptation, and the morning she was found unconscious — to anchor the discussion that follows.

Students work individually on the four brief-answer questions from “Let us discuss” (p.209) covering Sven's scientific reason, Claribel's adjustment, the mistaken intercom sound, and the canary-trouble prediction; pairs compare answers before a whole-class check.

Work through the seven true/false statements from “Let us discuss” (p.211) as a guided whole-class activity: teacher reads each statement, students hold up thumbs for true or false, then justify their verdict with a line from the text.

Close with a reflective question to the class: what detail in the story first signals that something is seriously wrong? Students share one-sentence responses; teacher notes recurring ideas on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often state that Claribel was part of an official experiment — the story is explicit that she was smuggled aboard for Sven's personal curiosity, and this misconception should be corrected during the brief-answer discussion. The true/false on the alarm circuit works well when students are asked to cite the exact passage, reinforcing close reading habits. The homework extract on Sven's construction work is self-contained and does not depend on class discussion to attempt.

periods.activity_title: The Warning in the Air: Extract Analysis and Deeper Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.213): Extract 2 — the Jim dialogue; four questions on air warning and imagery.
Let us think and reflect (p.213): three extended-answer questions — alarm purpose, crew reaction arc, problem-solving theme.

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 2 — the Jim dialogue beginning “Jim! There’s something wrong with the air!” — aloud together, then work through all four questions: the canary-miners comparison, Jim's confidence, 'shook Jim', and the oxygen-bottle simile; students discuss in pairs before class verification.

Students write individual responses to three extended questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.213): the purpose and failure of the alarm, how the crew's attitude toward Claribel shifts across the story, and what the ending suggests about low-tech problem-solving in high-tech environments.

Whole-class discussion: volunteers share their responses to the theme question; teacher draws out the contrast between the half-million-dollar engineering failure and Claribel's instinctive warning, and writes the central phrase — “unexpected, low-tech solutions” — on the board.

Teacher briefly names three remaining extended questions — title justification, uncertainty of life in space, humour in science fiction — as rich self-study paths for students who want to explore further, without allocating class time to them.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'shook Jim' is the most productive language point in Extract 2 — ensure students move beyond the literal reading (physically shaken) to the idiomatic one (startled by unwelcome information). The three remaining extended questions on the title, the 'slightly dead' line, and Clarke's humour are rich but cannot be anchored in the available time; flag them as self-study for students who want to go deeper into Clarke's craft. The air-purifier failure caused by an eclipse of Earth's shadow is a science-fiction detail worth naming explicitly so students understand the mechanism.

periods.activity_title: Martian Conversations: Listening Response and Silent-Letter Speaking

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.217): tick/cross five statements while listening to the Monika–Toby conversation.
Let us listen (p.218): fill five blanks with exact words from the conversation on second listen.
Let us speak (p.—): read words with silent letters aloud; circle the unpronounced letters.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Monika–Toby scenario briefly: a Martian stranded on Earth, befriended by Monika. Students prepare their tick/cross sheet for the five true/false statements in “Let us listen” (p.217).

Teacher reads the Monika–Toby transcript aloud at natural conversational pace; students mark tick or cross against each statement as they listen, then compare with a neighbour before the class verifies each answer.

Second reading of the transcript for the gap-fill in “Let us listen” (p.218): students write the exact words they hear in each blank — people, Martians/energy, chocolates, one, clouds/metals — then the class reads the filled sentences back aloud for rhythm check.

Move to “Let us speak”: teacher models the four story words — ballet, alarm, whistle, psychologist — exaggerating the silent letter then erasing it with voice; students repeat, circle the silent letter in each word, then extend to the ten additional words (receipt, debris, pneumonia, island, wreck, aisle, almond, campaign, foreign, fasten) in an unhurried paired read-aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Students almost always predict that Toby misses his school rather than his people — statement 1 in the tick/cross list is the most frequent error, worth pausing on. For the silent-letter activity, the most reliable pitfall is 'alarm': students expect the 'l' to be silent because of 'ballet', but in 'alarm' it is fully voiced — draw this contrast explicitly. The gap-fill words should be confirmed against the transcript text so students see that exact wording, not paraphrase, is the listening target.

periods.activity_title: Advice in Space and Writing for the Web

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.—): paired role-play — ask for and give advice on solar-system model and Chandrayaan-3 quiz.
Let us write (p.—): complete the internet social media web, then draft and revise a three-paragraph article on the importance of the internet.

time_bands.activity: Pairs enact the two advice-seeking situations from “Let us speak” — solar-system model materials and Chandrayaan-3 quiz preparation — using the prompt phrases on the board; teacher circulates, listening for register accuracy and ensuring both partners take each role.
Quick whole-class debrief: one pair demonstrates each scenario; class notes two phrases for asking advice and two for giving advice that felt natural and appropriately formal.

Introduce the article task from “Let us write”: teacher models filling the social media web — brainstorming uses of the internet (education, communication, entertainment, commerce) — and students complete their own webs individually, selecting four or five uses as paragraph anchors.

Students draft their article in three paragraphs following the given structure: general introduction, uses with examples, closing comment or quote; teacher circulates and offers brief formative nudges — a missing example, an abrupt ending, a heading not in place.

Students do a quick self-check: heading, name of writer, three paragraphs, a closing thought. A volunteer reads the opening sentence of their introduction aloud; teacher reinforces the formal article register before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: In the speaking task, students tend to keep both roles informal even when the prompt requires a school-project register — explicitly name the audience (a classmate, a teacher) before each scenario to anchor the level of formality. For the article, the most common structural gap is a missing closing statement; ensure students know the third paragraph should leave the reader with an idea, not merely list another use. The entire article — web, draft, and self-check — is completed within this sitting so no piece of writing is carried forward.
materials: Textbook — Feathered Friend, speaking and writing sections

periods.activity_title: Words That Merge, Adjectives That Fit, and Future Forms

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.214): match eight adjectives from the story text to the correct noun collocations.
Let us learn (p.214): combine word pairs into merged words and write the meaning of each.
Let us learn (p.216): fill eight blanks with the correct future-time verb form.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.217): fill six blanks in the AI paragraph with correct future-time verb forms.

time_bands.activity: Students match the eight adjectives — nagging, vague, delighted, narrow, sluggish, hushed, inexplicable, sheepish — to their noun collocations in “Let us learn” (p.214), then scan the story text to underline the sentence where each adjective actually appears; pairs compare findings.

Teacher introduces merged words using the story's own example, 'intercom' from 'internal' and 'communication'; students combine the six pairs in “Let us learn” (p.214) — motel, smog, sitcom, vlog, spork, webinar — and write a brief meaning beside each new word.

Teach the future-time reference table from “Let us learn” (p.215–216): simple present for schedules, present progressive for arrangements, 'going to' for intentions, 'will' for predictions; students complete the eight-blank exercise (p.216) individually, then the class verifies each answer with a reason.

Teacher previews the AI-paragraph exercise (p.217) as homework: students are to apply the same four future-time forms to a new context; a brief model of the first blank is done together so students understand the task before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The merged-word task works best when students articulate why the two source words belong together — 'smoke' and 'fog' share atmospheric density, 'spoon' and 'fork' share function — rather than just concatenating syllables. For the future-time grammar, the hardest distinction at this stage is 'going to' versus 'will': use sentences 4 and 8 from the exercise as the teaching pair, since both express a personal plan but at different certainty levels. The AI-paragraph homework (p.217) is self-contained and does not require class discussion to complete.

periods.activity_title: Canaries, Calamities, and Conservation: Exploring Beyond the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.—): read and discuss animal early-warning examples; evaluate the claim with evidence.
Let us explore (p.—): work in groups to plan and make a bird feeder using available classroom materials.

time_bands.activity: Students read the animal early-warning examples from “Let us explore” — elephants, flamingos, dogs before the 2004 tsunami; geese and sheep before the 1805 Naples earthquake; migratory birds and storms; sharks and dolphins before hurricanes — then work in groups of three to decide: is the claim that animals can sense natural calamities supported by the evidence? Each group prepares a one-sentence verdict.

Groups share their verdicts; teacher draws the parallel back to Claribel's role in the story — an animal whose biological sensitivity saved human lives — connecting the beyond-text reading to the narrative's central theme.

Groups of four design and build a simple bird feeder from “Let us explore” using cardboard, chart paper, and available classroom materials; teacher circulates, prompting each group to name one bird species it aims to attract and to label the feeder's key features.

Each group holds up its feeder and gives a twenty-second explanation of one design choice; teacher closes by noting that conserving birds — real feathered friends — carries the same spirit as the story's wry recommendation to welcome birdsong aboard a space station.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat the animal early-warning examples as folklore rather than documented behaviour — encourage them to notice that the examples span multiple continents and disaster types, which strengthens the claim. For the bird-feeder task, the making and presenting must both happen in this sitting; no materials should be taken away to finish later. Salim Ali and the coal-mine canary reading from “Let us explore” are rich self-study pointers for students who want to go further — flag them briefly without consuming class time.

items.source_lo: Student identifies explicit and implicit information in a narrative text using close reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Claribel's smuggling aboard, Sven's scientific curiosity, air-purifier failure, canary early-warning parallel.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below and mark each True or False.
1. Sven smuggled Claribel aboard the space station to conduct an officially approved science experiment.
2. The air-purifier froze because the station passed through the shadow of Earth during a rare eclipse.
3. The duty engineer Jim immediately accepted the narrator's warning that the air supply was failing.
4. The crew revived Claribel by giving her oxygen from an emergency cylinder.

options.text: Sven smuggled Claribel aboard the space station to conduct an officially approved science experiment.
The air-purifier froze because the station passed through the shadow of Earth during a rare eclipse.
The crew revived Claribel by giving her oxygen from an emergency cylinder.
The duty engineer Jim immediately accepted the narrator's warning that the air supply was failing.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — Claribel was brought aboard for Sven's personal scientific curiosity, not an official experiment. 2. True — the air purifier froze during a rare eclipse of Earth's shadow. 3. False — Jim dismissed the warning, confident the duplicate alarm circuits would have sounded; only his assistant's revelation that the second circuit was unconnected changed his mind. 4. True — the crew used oxygen from an emergency cylinder to revive Claribel.

items.source_lo: Student identifies explicit and implicit information in a narrative text using close reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Claribel's smuggling aboard, Sven's scientific curiosity, air-purifier failure, canary early-warning parallel.
items.item_stem: The narrator of the story ends with a wry recommendation: a visitor who hears birdsong on a space station should feel reassured rather than alarmed. What does this ending reveal about the narrator's view of the relationship between low-technology solutions and high-technology environments? Support your answer with at least one specific detail from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The narrator suggests that a simple, living creature can outperform elaborate engineering in a critical situation — Claribel detected the failing air supply when half a million dollars of equipment, including a disconnected alarm circuit, could not. The wry tone of the ending implies that the narrator values practical ingenuity over technological confidence, and that a small canary at almost no extra cost proved more reliable than the station's duplicate alarm system.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a scripted conversation and retrieves accurate detail using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Monika and Toby dialogue: Martian biology, single eye, solar energy, X-ray vision, Monika's breakfast.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Monika and Toby and choose the correct answer for each question.
1. What does Toby say Martians use as their source of energy?
A. Food and water
B. The Sun
C. Air
D. Electricity

2. How many eyes does Toby have, and what unusual claim does he make about his vision?
A. Two eyes; he can see in complete darkness.
B. One eye; he can see through mountains, clouds, wood, and metals.
C. One eye; he can read minds.
D. Two eyes; he can see beyond the stars.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this assume Martians share human biological needs, missing Toby's explicit statement about solar energy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests a guess based on the space-station context of the chapter rather than careful listening to Toby's words.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates students confused a plausible science-fiction detail with what Toby actually says in the transcript.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a scripted conversation and retrieves accurate detail using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Monika and Toby dialogue: Martian biology, single eye, solar energy, X-ray vision, Monika's breakfast.
items.item_stem: At the end of the conversation, Toby reveals two things he can perceive about Monika without her telling him. What are they, and what do these revelations suggest about how Toby experiences the world differently from humans? Write your answer in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Toby reveals that Monika has a blue toy aeroplane in her pocket and that the apple she ate for breakfast is moving around in her stomach — details he perceives with his single eye even though they are hidden from normal sight. These revelations suggest that Toby's single eye functions as an X-ray or penetrating sense, allowing him to see through solid objects and inside Monika's body, an ability completely outside human sensory experience.

items.item_stem: You want to create a model of the solar system for your school's Science Exhibition, but you are unsure what materials to use. Speak with a classmate: ask for advice clearly, respond to at least one suggestion your partner gives, and together decide on a final plan. Speak for about one minute each.

expected_elements: Uses at least one advice-seeking phrase (What should I use…? How can I…?).
Responds to partner's suggestion with agreement, question, or counter-suggestion.
Maintains school-appropriate register throughout the exchange.
Reaches a shared decision on materials before closing.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Monika from the listening conversation. You have just met Toby and are astonished by his abilities. Role-play a scene in which you ask Toby for advice on how to prepare for your inter-class science quiz. Express your opinion about whether his suggestions would actually help you, and give a reason for your view. Speak for about one minute.

expected_elements: Adopts Monika's curious, friendly tone established in the transcript.
Asks Toby for at least one specific piece of advice about quiz preparation.
States a personal opinion on whether Toby's advice is useful, with a reason.
Uses at least one opinion phrase (I think…, In my view…, I feel…).

items.item_stem: A student magazine has asked you to write a short article. Write the opening paragraph of an article titled 'The Importance of the Internet'. Your paragraph should introduce the topic to a general reader, name at least two ways the internet is used, and end with a sentence that encourages the reader to keep reading. Use a heading and write your name below it.

expected_elements: Heading 'The Importance of the Internet' and writer's name present.
Opening sentence introduces the internet to a general reader.
Names at least two distinct uses (e.g. education, communication).
Closing sentence of the paragraph hooks the reader to continue.

items.item_stem: Write a complete three-paragraph article titled 'The Importance of the Internet'. In your first paragraph, introduce the topic. In your second paragraph, explain at least three uses of the internet with specific examples. In your third paragraph, share your own opinion about the internet's role in the future and end with a thoughtful idea or quote. Use a heading and include your name.

expected_elements: All three structural elements present: introduction, uses, closing opinion.
At least three uses supported by concrete, specific examples.
Third paragraph contains a personal viewpoint, not merely another use.
Closes with a thoughtful idea, question, or quote — not a list item.
Formal article register maintained; heading and writer's name included.

items.source_context: Story adjectives and collocations, merged words from 'intercom', future-time verb forms (will, going to, simple present, present progressive).
items.item_stem:
The word 'intercom' in 'Feathered Friend' is a merged word formed from 'internal' and 'communication'. Use your knowledge of future-time verb forms to complete the passage below. Choose from: simple present, present progressive, 'will', or 'going to'. Write the complete verb form in each blank.

The science club has made several plans for next term. Their first event (1) __________ (start) on Monday — it is already in the timetable. The president announced yesterday that the club (2) __________ (launch) a school podcast about space exploration. In the podcast, student reporters (3) __________ (interview) their science teacher every fortnight. One reporter said, 'I (4) __________ (prepare) my questions tonight so I am ready.' The club believes the podcast (5) __________ (inspire) younger students to take up science as a hobby.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. starts (simple present — fixed schedule); 2. is going to launch (going to — announced intention); 3. will interview (will — prediction/plan stated as fact); 4. am going to prepare (going to — personal intention decided now); 5. will inspire (will — prediction about the future).

items.source_context: Animal early-warning examples across disasters; bird conservation; making a simple bird feeder.
items.item_stem: In 'Feathered Friend', Claribel the canary warns the crew of a life-threatening danger before the station's alarms can. Write an extended response in which you: (a) describe how this fictional event connects to the real-world practice of using canaries in coal mines to detect dangerous gases, and (b) explain what both examples — the coal mine and the space station — suggest about the relationship between animal sensitivity and human safety. Use at least one specific detail from the story in your response.

expected_elements: Names the coal-mine practice: canaries detect carbon monoxide and warn miners.
Links Claribel's unconsciousness to the same biological principle.
Uses a specific story detail (e.g. 'slightly dead', alarm circuit unconnected).
States a clear idea about animal sensitivity as a reliable safety tool.

items.item_stem: Design a bird conservation project for your school. Your project should: (a) name at least two bird species found in your region that face threats, (b) propose one practical action your school community can take to help those birds (such as building feeders, planting native trees, or reducing window collisions), and (c) explain how your project connects to the theme of 'Feathered Friend' — that living creatures deserve protection because of the value they bring to other lives. Present your plan as a short written proposal with a title, a goal statement, and at least two action steps.

expected_elements: Names at least two regionally relevant bird species under threat.
Proposes a specific, school-feasible conservation action.
Connects the project explicitly to the story's theme of animal value.
Written as a proposal: title, goal statement, and at least two action steps.
